A.q: Which of the following is the cleanest definition of a physical quantity?
options: A unit written with no numerical value
A measured property with a number and a unit
A property seen without any measurement
A solid object that merely occupies space
A.explain: A physical quantity is a measurable property written as a number times a unit, as in 10 kg or 37 °C. A bare unit, an unmeasured observation, and a mere object do not complete that pair.

A.q: How many base quantities does the SI system have, and what is the SI unit of temperature?
A.explain: The SI system has 7 base quantities, and temperature's base unit is the kelvin The seven are: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), temperature (K), electric current (A), luminous intensity (Cd), amount of substance (mol). Notice temperature is kelvin, not Celsius, Celsius is a derived scale defined from kelvin (0 °C = 273.15 K). In medical physics calculations, always convert to kelvin first

A.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity, not a base quantity?
A.explain: Area = length × length, so it is built from base quantities and is derived Derived quantities are made from base quantities by multiplication or division. Examples: Area = L²; Speed = L/T; Force = M·L/T² (= newton); Pressure = M/(L·T²) (= pascal). Mass, time, and length are all base, they can't be reduced further. You can spot derived quantities because their units are combinations (m², m/s, kg·m/s²).

A.q: In the CGS system, the units of length, mass, and time are:
A.explain: CGS = centimetre - gram - second. FPS = foot - pound - second. MKS = metre - kilogram - second. The letters in each name are the units themselves: CGS is centimetre, gram, second; FPS is foot, pound, second; MKS is metre, kilogram, second. SI is the modern international standard and uses the MKS structure (metre, kilogram, second) plus the other four base units. Medical physics uses SI almost exclusively.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT matter?
A.explain: Matter must have mass and occupy space. Light has neither rest mass nor volume, it is not matter Light is electromagnetic radiation, photons are massless and take up no volume, so they don't count as matter even though they carry energy and momentum. Bone (solid), blood (liquid), and air in the lungs (gas) are all matter. This is why we can say 'matter is everywhere in the human body', every tissue is matter, but the signals and radiation passing through it are not.

A.q: Rank the intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest across the three common states:
A.explain: Solids hold their molecules most tightly, gases least tightly Strong intermolecular forces explain why solids are rigid and cannot be compressed. Weak forces explain why gases expand to fill any container and compress easily. In the body: bone molecules are locked in a rigid lattice (strong IMF); blood molecules slide past each other (moderate IMF); air molecules zip around freely (weak IMF). This is why gas exchange in lungs relies on volume change, but bone can support your body weight.

A.q: Which ordering of diffusion rate is correct?
options: Diffusion is equal in all three
A.explain: Diffusion is fastest in gases because their molecules move fastest and are furthest apart Diffusion = movement of particles from high concentration to low concentration. Gases: fast (perfume fills a room in seconds). Liquids: slower (food colouring in water takes minutes). Solids: extremely slow (dye in ice barely moves at all). Medical application: oxygen diffuses rapidly from alveoli into blood (gas-to-liquid) but the transport of oxygen around the whole body depends on bulk flow (blood circulation), not diffusion alone

A.q: Kinetic energy of particles is temperature-dependent. Which statement is correct?
options: Kinetic energy does not depend on temperature
Solids have the highest kinetic energy
Gases have the highest kinetic energy
All three states have equal kinetic energy
A.explain: At a given temperature, gases have the highest particle kinetic energy and solids the lowest. Solid particles mainly vibrate in place; liquid particles slide; gas particles move rapidly. Temperature measures average kinetic energy.

A.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes elasticity from plasticity?
options: Elasticity deforms permanently; plasticity returns to shape
Elasticity returns to shape; plasticity deforms permanently
Elasticity and plasticity both return to the original shape
Elasticity and plasticity both leave a permanent set
A.explain: Elasticity is recovery of shape after the load is removed. Plasticity is the permanent set that remains. Swapping the two, or giving both the same outcome, reverses or erases that split.

A.q: What is the difference between ductility and malleability?
options: Ductility means sheets; malleability means wires
Ductility and malleability both mean compressibility
Ductility and malleability both mean fracture resistance
Ductility means wires; malleability means sheets
A.explain: Ductility is drawing into thin wires. Malleability is hammering or rolling into sheets. The swapped pair, and the two shared meanings, are not that split.

A.q: Stress is defined as:
A.explain: Stress = F / A. SI unit: N/m² = Pascal (Pa) Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area that develops in response to an external force. Same force on a smaller area = higher stress. This is why thin bones (osteoporosis) fracture more easily than thick ones under the same body weight: F is the same but A is smaller, so stress = F/A is larger. Also why a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one: the same force concentrated on a tiny area generates enormous stress.

A.q: Strain is best described as:
options: Same quantity as stress, units of pascal
Relative length change, with no units
Force per unit area, units of pascal
Force times area, units of newton metre
A.explain: Strain is the deformation divided by the original dimension, so the units cancel. Stress is force per area in pascals, and force times area is not a strain.

A.q: Hooke's Law states that stress and strain are proportional up to which point?
options: The breaking point of the loaded specimen
The melting point of the loaded specimen
The boiling point of the loaded specimen
A.explain: Hooke's law holds while stress stays proportional to strain, which ends at the proportional limit (also called the elastic limit). The breaking point is later, and melting or boiling are thermal changes, not that limit.

A.q: Which of the following is a medical example of stress in the human body?
options: Blood pressure acting on vessel walls
Light passing through the lens of the eye
Sound travelling along the ear canal
A.explain: Blood pressure on a vessel wall is force per area, which is stress. Light, sound, and photosynthesis are not that force on a surface.

A.q: Which state of matter is described as having a definite size and shape and being unable to be compressed?
A.explain: Solids have definite shape and volume, high density, strong intermolecular forces, and cannot be compressed Bone is the medical example of a solid: rigid, definite shape, cannot be compressed. Compare: liquids (blood) have no definite shape but a nearly fixed volume, and are not easily compressible; gases (air in the lungs) have neither definite shape nor volume and are easily compressible. This hierarchy is why the skeleton (solid) can support the body while the bloodstream (liquid) can flow and the lungs (gas) can expand and contract with each breath.

A.q: Which of the following is an additional state of matter beyond solid, liquid, and gas?
A.explain: Beyond solid, liquid, and gas, the additional state named here is the Bose-Einstein condensate. Vapour, ice, and steam are ordinary phases of water, not a further state.

A.q: Which statement about ideal liquids is correct?
options: Ideal liquids compress fully, and they exist in nature
Ideal liquids do not compress, and none exist in nature
Ideal liquids exist in nature as pure water alone
Ideal liquids outpull solids in intermolecular force
A.explain: An ideal liquid is defined as incompressible, and no real liquid meets that ideal. Compressibility, pure water, and a stronger force than solids are not that definition.

A.q: Which of the following is not one of the five mechanical properties?
A.explain: The five mechanical properties are elasticity, plasticity, ductility, malleability, and strength. Conductivity is an electrical/thermal property Conductivity describes how well a material transmits heat or electricity, that's an electrical/thermal property, not a mechanical one. Mechanical properties describe how a material responds to forces: does it return to shape (elastic), deform permanently (plastic), draw into wires (ductile), hammer into sheets (malleable), or resist failure (strength)? Bone's mechanical properties are what let it bear load; its electrical properties (if any) would be a different chapter.

A.q: A bone that bends slightly under load and returns to its original shape when the load is removed is displaying:
A.explain: Elasticity = returns to original shape after force removal. This is normal bone behaviour under physiological loads Bone is actually both: elastic under small loads (walking, mild exercise) and plastic under extreme loads (a fall, repeated overloading). Under normal walking, bone flexes by a fraction of a millimetre and returns fully. Under marathon-level repetitive loading, it enters the plastic zone and develops stress fractures. This dual behaviour is why rest days are important for athletes, they allow bone to recover before plastic damage accumulates.

A.q: What happens when a material is loaded beyond its elastic limit?
options: It returns to its original shape
A.explain: Beyond the elastic limit, deformation becomes permanent. Continue loading and the material reaches its breaking point The stress-strain curve past the elastic limit flattens (plastic region), the material keeps deforming without much additional stress. Remove the force and it stays deformed. Examples: bending a paperclip, stretching a rubber band too far, overloading a bone into a stress fracture. Complete failure occurs at the breaking point, where the material fractures, tears, or shatters.

A.q: Which of the following correctly reports a measured mass as a physical quantity?
A.explain: A measured mass needs a number and the mass unit. 10 kg has both. 5 N is a force, 10 m is a length, and 5 Pa is a pressure; each has a number and a unit but none reports mass.

A.q: Pressure on teeth during chewing is an example of:
A.explain: Chewing presses force onto the tooth face, which is stress, force per area. Diffusion, sublimation, and elasticity name other properties and are not what that bite applies.

A.q: Which statement about solids is FALSE?
A.explain: Solids are NOT easily compressed, strong intermolecular forces lock particles in place That's why you can't push your hand through a table or compress a bone. Molecules in a solid are packed tightly with strong IMF, so pushing them closer requires enormous pressure. Gases, with weak IMF and large spacing, compress easily (that's why a syringe can compress air but not water). In the body, the incompressibility of bone is what allows it to support the weight of everything above it

A.q: Malleability is the property of being:
A.explain: Malleable = can be hammered/rolled into sheets. Ductile = can be drawn into wires Gold is famously malleable, a single gram can be hammered into a sheet of about 1 m². Copper is ductile, it's drawn into the wires in your house. Both require atoms to slide past each other without breaking bonds, but 'malleable' means the deformation is compression into flat sheets, while 'ductile' means the deformation is tension into thin wires. Bone is neither, because its mineral structure resists both kinds of deformation.

A.q: The strength of a material refers to its ability to:
A.explain: Strength is the ability to carry applied stress without failure. Bending without fracture is closer to toughness, and conduction or dissolving are not mechanical strength.

A.q: A bone under 9 × 10⁶ Pa of stress shows a strain of 0.003. What is the Young's modulus of this sample?
A.explain: Y = stress / strain = (9×10⁶) / (3×10⁻³) = 3 × 10⁹ Pa = 3 GPa. That's 3 GPa, between typical cancellous bone and cortical bone (cortical bone is often about 15–20 GPa). The formula is just Y = stress / strain, the slope of the linear (elastic) portion of the stress-strain curve. If you plot stress on the y-axis and strain on the x-axis, Young's modulus is the slope of the straight line before the material yields.

A.q: Blood in the human body is best classified as which state of matter?
A.explain: Blood behaves as a liquid: no definite shape, nearly fixed volume, moderate intermolecular forces, not easily compressible Technically blood is a suspension of cells in plasma, but it is the working example of a liquid. Its key liquid properties: takes the shape of its container (arteries, veins), has a nearly fixed volume at constant pressure, and cannot be easily compressed. This is why pressure waves (the pulse) travel through blood so predictably, the liquid is nearly incompressible, so the pressure transmits almost instantly along the vessel.

A.q: Which of the following is not one of the four unit systems?
A.explain: The four unit systems are CGS, FPS, MKS, and SI. GPS is a positioning system, not a unit system. CGS: centimetre-gram-second. FPS: foot-pound-second. MKS: metre-kilogram-second. SI: International System of Units, the modern standard with 7 base units. GPS (Global Positioning System) is a navigation technology. SI is the modern descendant of MKS; they share metre, kilogram, and second as base units.

A.q: What is the constant of proportionality between stress and strain called?
A.explain: Modulus of elasticity = Stress / Strain. It is a material property within the elastic limit The same material has the same modulus regardless of sample size. Steel has a Young's modulus of about 200 GPa whether it is a wire or a bridge beam. That is what makes modulus useful: it lets you compare materials independently of the shape you happen to be testing.

A.q: Which formula correctly represents the modulus of elasticity?
A.explain: Modulus = Stress / Strain. Units: pascal (Pa), because strain is dimensionless If 100 MPa of stress produces 0.0005 strain, modulus = 100×10⁶ / 5×10⁻⁴ = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa = 200 GPa, the modulus of steel. Larger modulus = stiffer material = more stress needed to deform it.

A.q: How many types of modulus of elasticity exist, and what are they?
options: Four: tensile, compressive, shear, and torsional
One: Young's modulus, with no further type
Two: a linear modulus and a nonlinear modulus
Three: Young's, shear, and bulk modulus
A.explain: Three moduli follow the three loadings: Young's for longitudinal strain, shear modulus for shear strain, and bulk modulus for volume strain. Four named loadings, a single modulus, or a linear-nonlinear split are not that set.

A.q: Longitudinal stress is applied:
options: At the two end faces alone
Along the long axis of the object
A.explain: Longitudinal stress is applied along the axis, stretching or compressing the length. A parallel force is shear, equal pressure from all sides is hydraulic stress, and end faces alone do not define the loading.

A.q: Longitudinal strain is calculated as:
A.explain: Longitudinal strain = ΔL / L, where ΔL is the change in length and L is the original length. It is dimensionless Bone length 0.20 m stretched to 0.20012 m. ΔL = 0.00012 m. Strain = 0.00012 / 0.20 = 0.0006. No units. This is the exact strain used in the cortical bone problem, and it is the same ratio no matter how long the specimen is.

A.q: Young's modulus is calculated as:
A.explain: Young's modulus = Longitudinal stress / Longitudinal strain = (F/A) / (ΔL/L). Units: Pa Young's modulus is the slope of the linear (elastic) part of a stress-strain graph. Steeper slope = stiffer material. Diamond has a Young's modulus of about 1000 GPa, extremely stiff. Rubber has a Young's modulus of about 0.01 GPa, very compliant. Bone sits at around 16 GPa, between the two.

A.q: Shear strain is calculated as:
A.explain: Shear strain = Δx / L, where Δx is the horizontal displacement of one face and L is the perpendicular height Push the top of a thick book sideways, the top cover slides by Δx while the bottom stays put. Shear strain = Δx divided by height. No units, it is a ratio of two lengths, like all strains.

A.q: Shear modulus is calculated as:
A.explain: Shear modulus = Shear stress / Shear strain = (F/A) / (Δx/L). Units: Pa When you twist a rod, each cross-section rotates relative to the one below, that is shear. The shear modulus tells you how much twist you get for a given torque. Metals have a high shear modulus (steel ≈ 80 GPa); rubber has a low shear modulus (≈ 1 MPa), which is why rubber is easy to twist.

A.q: Bulk modulus is calculated as:
A.explain: Bulk modulus = Hydraulic stress / Hydraulic strain = (F/A) / (ΔV/V). Units: Pa A balloon underwater shrinks in volume without changing shape. Pressure P = F/A produces a fractional volume change ΔV/V. The ratio is the bulk modulus. Water has a bulk modulus of about 2.2 GPa, extremely hard to compress. Gases have a small bulk modulus, which is why they compress easily.

A.q: Hydraulic (volume) stress is:
options: Uniform pressure inward from all sides
A tangential force along the surface
A single force applied at one point
A lengthwise force along the object axis
A.explain: Hydraulic stress is a uniform pressure applied from all sides by a fluid. A tangential force is shear, a point force is not a volume stress, and a lengthwise force is longitudinal.

A.q: Larger the Young's modulus of a material means:
options: Less stress is required to produce a small deformation
More stress is required to produce a small change in length
A.explain: Higher Young's modulus = stiffer material. More stress is required for the same strain Steel (Young's modulus ≈ 200 GPa) vs rubber (Young's modulus ≈ 0.01 GPa). To stretch a steel rod by 0.1% takes 20,000× more stress than stretching rubber by the same fraction. Bone's Young's modulus (~16 GPa) puts it much closer to steel, bone is stiff enough to bear the body's weight without sagging.

A.q: Cortical bone specimen: L = 0.25 m, A = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m², F = 1500 N, ΔL = 0.15 mm. Calculate the Young's modulus.
A.explain: Stress = F/A = 1500 / 2.0×10⁻⁴ = 7.5×10⁶ Pa. Strain = ΔL/L = 1.5×10⁻⁴ / 0.25 = 6.0×10⁻⁴. Young's modulus Y = stress/strain = 7.5×10⁶ / 6.0×10⁻⁴ = 1.25×10¹⁰ Pa.

A.q: Femur: L = 0.45 m, Young's modulus = 18×10⁹ Pa, max stress = 120×10⁶ Pa. Find maximum compression ΔL before breaking.
A.explain: Strain = stress / Young's modulus = 120×10⁶ / 18×10⁹ = 1/150 ≈ 0.00667. ΔL = strain × L = 0.00667 × 0.45 = 0.00300 m = 3.00 mm. A 45 cm femur can compress by only about 3 mm before reaching its breaking stress, under 1% of its length. That narrow margin is why a fall from standing height can break a hip in an elderly patient: the load exceeds the stress limit, and the small elastic range is quickly exceeded.

A.q: What are the units of strain?
A.explain: Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no units. Pascal and newton per square metre belong to stress, and newton and metre are base or derived units of force and length.

A.q: What happens to a material loaded beyond its elastic limit?
options: It becomes more elastic than before
It loses mass but keeps its shape
It returns fully to its old shape
A.explain: Past the elastic limit the deformation is permanent, and further load leads to break. Recovery of shape belongs inside the limit, and the load does not add elasticity or remove mass.

A.q: A cylinder is stretched lengthwise by a change in length ΔL. This loading represents:
options: Shear stress across the side face
A.explain: A lengthwise stretch is tensile longitudinal stress. Compression shortens the length, shear slides the face, and hydraulic stress pushes from every side.

A.q: A cylinder has its top face displaced sideways by Δx while the base stays fixed. This loading represents:
A.explain: Force parallel to the surface causing sliding is shear stress. The cylinder deforms like a pack of playing cards pushed sideways Notice the height L doesn't change, only the horizontal displacement Δx changes. That is the hallmark of shear: no length change, only angular distortion. Shear stress is what your vertebral discs experience when you rotate your torso.

A.q: A sphere shrinks in volume under pressure applied by a surrounding fluid. This loading represents:
A.explain: Uniform pressure applied from all directions producing a volume change ΔV without shape change is hydraulic stress (also called volume stress). It is isotropic and can only change volume, never shape. Shear, tensile, and longitudinal stress are directional loadings.

A.q: When a bone bends, the side being compressed is under ______ stress, while the side being stretched is under ______ stress.
A.explain: When a long bone bends, one side is squeezed (compressive) and the opposite side is stretched (tensile). Both are forms of longitudinal stress This is why long bones typically fracture on the tension side first, bone is weaker in tension than in compression. Clinically, this is why a bending force on a limb produces a fracture that starts on the side being stretched. diagram labels both regions, plus the fracture point.

A.q: How does osteoporosis affect the Young's modulus of bone?
options: It increases bone mass, not the modulus
It raises the modulus and stiffens bone
It lowers the modulus and embrittles bone
It leaves the modulus entirely unchanged
A.explain: Osteoporosis lowers Young's modulus, so less stress produces the same strain and the bone fractures more readily. It does not raise stiffness, leave the modulus alone, or act only by adding mass.

A.q: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a condition in which:
options: Bones have an unusually high Young's modulus
Bones are brittle with lower Young's modulus
Joints fail while bone modulus stays normal
Bones become more elastic than normal bone
A.explain: Osteogenesis imperfecta leaves bone brittle, with a lower Young's modulus and easy fracture. The modulus is not raised, the defect is not confined to joints, and the bone is not more elastic.

A.q: Loss of elasticity in blood vessels is significant because it:
options: It improves the circulation in the vessel
It changes the vein diameter alone
It leaves the circulation clinically unchanged
A.explain: Loss of vessel elasticity is linked with cardiovascular disease. It does not improve circulation, act on vein diameter alone, or leave the circulation unchanged.

A.q: Which pairing of stress and unit is correct?
A.explain: Stress = Force / Area, so its SI unit is the pascal (Pa) = N/m². Strain is dimensionless; joule and metre are not stress units. Stress and pressure share the pascal because both are force per unit area.

A.q: The modulus of elasticity reflects which property of a material?
A.explain: The modulus of elasticity is stress divided by strain, so it measures stiffness, the resistance to deformation. Color, temperature, and conductivity are unrelated.

A.q: Tensile stress applied to a material causes it to:
A.explain: Tensile stress pulls the material along its axis, causing elongation (stretching) The word 'tensile' shares a root with 'tension', both imply pulling. A muscle pulling on its tendon is tensile stress on that tendon. Compressive stress is the opposite: pushing ends together, shortening the object. Both produce ΔL, but with opposite signs. Both are forms of longitudinal stress.

A.q: Compressive stress applied to a material causes it to:
A.explain: Compressive stress pushes the ends together, shortening the material. It is a form of longitudinal stress The femur problem is a compressive stress example: the bone shortens slightly under load before it fractures. Bone is actually stronger in compression than in tension, that is why fractures usually start on the tension side of a bending bone, and why vertebral compression fractures are a hallmark of osteoporosis (the vertebrae are loaded in compression).

A.q: Shear deformation is described as being somewhat like:
options: A spring stretched along its length
A sponge soaking up added water
A pack of cards pushed sideways
A.explain: Shear slides layers sideways, like a pack of cards pushed at the top. A balloon and a sponge change volume, and a spring stretch is longitudinal strain.

A.q: Hydraulic stress produces which kind of deformation?
options: Both length and shape change together
Length change, with the shape held fixed
Angular distortion, with volume held fixed
Volume change, with the shape held fixed
A.explain: Hydraulic stress is a uniform pressure from all sides, so the volume changes and the shape does not. A length change is longitudinal, and an angular distortion is shear.

A.q: Why is the Young's modulus clinically useful for assessing bone health?
options: It records the surface color of bone
It tracks stiffness and fracture risk
It records the temperature of the bone
It records the chronological age of bone
A.explain: Young's modulus measures stiffness under elastic load, so a fall in it flags easier fracture. Color, temperature, and age are not what the modulus reports.

A.q: Which statement best explains why liquids and gases are both classified as fluids?
options: They flow and deform continuously under shear
They share one density at every temperature
They contain a single kind of molecule each
They keep a fixed shape under every load
A.explain: Liquids and gases are fluids because they flow from high pressure to low pressure and keep deforming under shear. They do not share one density, one molecular type, or a fixed shape.

A.q: The density (ρ) of an object is defined as:
A.explain: Density ρ = mass m / volume V. SI unit: kg/m³ Density is an intrinsic property: a litre of water and a cup of water have the same density. Mass and volume change with sample size, but their ratio does not. This is what makes density useful for identifying materials.

A.q: A block measures 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm and has a mass of 600 g. What is its density?
A.explain: Volume = 4 × 5 × 10 = 200 cm³. Density = 600 / 200 = 3.0 g/cm³. In SI units, this is 3000 kg/m³, about three times the density of water. The specific gravity of this block is 3.0.

A.q: A glass block measures 10 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm and has a density of 2.5 g/cm³. What is its mass?
A.explain: Volume = 10 × 4 × 5 = 200 cm³. Mass = density × volume = 2.5 × 200 = 500 g. Density and the block dimensions (which give volume) are known, so mass follows from rearranging ρ = m/V to m = ρV.

A.q: What is the specific gravity of a substance?
options: Mass of the sample divided by volume
Density of the sample divided by water
Volume of the sample divided by mass
Density of the sample multiplied by g
A.explain: Specific gravity is the density of the substance divided by the density of water, a ratio with no units. Mass over volume is density itself, volume over mass is its reciprocal, and multiplying by g produces a weight density.

A.q: How do you convert a density given in g/cm³ to kg/m³?
A.explain: Multiply by 1000. For example, 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ The factor of 1000 comes from the conversion of both mass (1 kg = 1000 g) and length (1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³). Combining: (1000 g / 10⁶ cm³) = 10⁻³ g/cm³ per kg/m³, which inverts to the multiplication factor of 1000. So 2 g/cm³ = 2000 kg/m³.

A.q: Pressure is defined as:
A.explain: Pressure P = Force / Area = mg / A. SI unit: pascal (Pa) = N/m² Pressure measures how concentrated a force is over a surface. The same force applied over a smaller area gives a larger pressure, this is why a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one. In fluids, pressure is the fundamental quantity that determines flow and forces on submerged objects.

A.q: In a static fluid, how does pressure behave at a given depth?
options: It acts downward at that depth
It acts upward at that depth
It acts equally in every direction
It acts sideways at that depth
A.explain: In a fluid at rest, pressure at one depth pushes equally in every direction. A single direction, down, up, or sideways, would set the fluid moving.

A.q: The force exerted by a fluid on a submerged object is always:
options: Perpendicular to the surface, rising with depth
Tangent to the surface, falling with depth
Absent from the surface at every depth
Parallel to the surface, constant with depth
A.explain: A fluid at rest pushes perpendicular to a surface, and that push grows with depth. A tangent or parallel force is shear, and the force is not zero.

A.q: Which expression gives the pressure at a depth h below the surface of a liquid of density ρ?
A.explain: P = ρgh. It is derived from P = F/A, substituting the weight of the fluid column above the depth h The derivation goes: P = mg/A. Mass = ρV = ρ(Ah). Substituting gives P = ρAhg/A = ρgh. The area cancels, which is why the pressure at a given depth depends only on the fluid and depth, not on the shape or size of the container

A.q: The pressure on an object at depth h in a liquid, measured from atmospheric level, is called:
A.explain: Gauge pressure P_G = ρgh. It measures the excess over atmospheric pressure Gauge pressure is what a diver's depth gauge reads. It ignores the atmospheric pressure already acting on the surface. Absolute pressure, by contrast, adds atmospheric pressure to gauge pressure: P_abs = P_atm + P_G.

A.q: At sea level, what is the value of standard atmospheric pressure in pascals?
A.explain: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 1.013 × 10⁵ N/m² This is roughly 101 kilopascals, or just over 1 bar. It is the pressure that a column of mercury 76 cm tall exerts at its base, which is exactly what the mercury barometer demonstrates. The reason we are not crushed by this pressure is that our internal pressure matches it

A.q: Which of the following is a correct equivalent for 1 atm?
A.explain: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 760 torr = 14.7 lb/in² The 760 torr value comes directly from the barometer: the mercury column is 760 mm (76 cm) tall. Torr and mmHg are identical units, both named after Torricelli. The lb/in² value is the imperial equivalent, useful in some medical and engineering contexts.

A.q: What is the purpose of the mercury barometer developed by Torricelli?
options: To measure the density of a fluid
To measure the buoyant force on a body
To measure the pressure of arterial blood
To measure the pressure of the atmosphere
A.explain: Torricelli's mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure from the height of the mercury column. Density, buoyancy, and arterial pressure are other measurements.

A.q: A mercury barometer shows a column of 70 cm. If water were used instead, approximately how tall would the column need to be?
A.explain: Mercury is about 13.6 times as dense as water, so the water column is 70 cm × 13.6 = 952 cm ≈ 9.5 m. The same result follows from h = P/(ρg): the 70 cm mercury column is a pressure of 13,600 × 9.8 × 0.70 = 9.33 × 10⁴ Pa, and 9.33 × 10⁴ / (1000 × 9.8) = 9.52 m. Mercury is preferred because a water barometer is inconveniently tall.

A.q: An open-tube manometer is used primarily to measure:
A.explain: The open-tube manometer measures gas pressure in a container. It is a U-shaped tube half-filled with a liquid One end connects to the container whose pressure is being measured; the other end is open to atmosphere. The difference in liquid heights on the two sides corresponds to the difference between the container pressure and atmospheric pressure, this is the gauge pressure.

A.q: Which equation correctly relates absolute pressure, atmospheric pressure, and gauge pressure?
A.explain: P_abs = P_atm + P_gauge. Absolute pressure is the sum of atmospheric and gauge pressure. If a tyre gauge reads 30 psi (gauge), the absolute pressure inside the tyre is about 44.7 psi (14.7 psi atmospheric + 30 psi gauge). Gauge pressure answers 'how much above atmosphere?', absolute pressure answers 'how much above vacuum?'.

A.q: In a manometer, the gauge pressure of a gas in a container is given by:
A.explain: Gauge pressure = ρgΔh, where Δh is the height difference between the two liquid levels in the manometer The height difference Δh is what the manometer physically measures. Multiplying by ρg converts that column height to a pressure. If the liquid level on the container side is lower, the container pressure exceeds atmospheric, the gauge pressure is positive. If it is higher, the container is under vacuum relative to atmosphere, the gauge pressure is negative.

A.q: A diver is at a depth where the gauge pressure reads 2.94 × 10⁵ Pa in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²). How deep is the diver?
A.explain: h = P_G / (ρg) = 2.94 × 10⁵ / (1000 × 9.8) = 30.0 m. The gauge pressure is about 2.9 atmospheres above the surface. At about 10.3 m, fresh water adds 1 atm of gauge pressure, so 30 m adds roughly 3 atm. Divers must ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness, a consequence of the physics of pressure at depth.

A.q: What is the absolute pressure at a depth of 15 m in fresh water, given ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², and P_atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa?
A.explain: P_gauge = 1000 × 9.8 × 15 = 1.47 × 10⁵ Pa. P_abs = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 1.47 × 10⁵ = 2.483 × 10⁵ Pa. Every 10 metres of fresh water adds about 1 atm of gauge pressure, so 15 m adds about 1.5 atm and the absolute pressure is about 2.5 atm.

A.q: Pascal's principle states that:
options: A pressure change is transmitted equally throughout
Pressure equals density times gravity times height
Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced
Pressure falls steadily as depth in the fluid rises
A.explain: Pascal's principle says an external pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid. Density times g times height is pressure at depth, buoyant force is Archimedes, and pressure rises, not falls, with depth.

A.q: A hydraulic system has a small piston of area 0.01 m² and a large piston of area 0.40 m². If 200 N is applied on the small piston, what is the output force on the large piston?
A.explain: F_out = F_in × (A_out / A_in) = 200 × (0.40 / 0.01) = 200 × 40 = 8000 N. The area ratio is 40:1, so the force is amplified 40 times. The small piston must move 40 times farther than the large piston: energy is conserved, but the force is multiplied.

A.q: The buoyant force on a submerged object arises because:
options: Gravity acts on the object alone
The fluid itself supplies the weight
Top and bottom pressures are unequal
The object's density supplies the force
A.explain: Pressure increases with depth, so the upward push on the bottom face exceeds the downward push on the top face. That difference is the buoyant force. Gravity, fluid weight, and object density do not by themselves name that difference.

A.q: Archimedes' Principle states that the magnitude of the buoyant force is equal to:
options: The weight of the submerged object itself
The weight of the fluid the object displaces
The mass of the object multiplied by g
The density of the object times its volume
A.explain: Archimedes' principle sets the buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. The object's own weight, its mass times g, and density times volume are not that displaced weight.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes a fluid?
options: It continuously deforms under shear stress
It maintains a fixed shape under shear
A.explain: A fluid is a substance that continuously deforms under shear stress This is the formal definition that distinguishes fluids from solids. A solid under shear deforms by a finite amount and then reaches equilibrium. A fluid under any nonzero shear stress continues to deform indefinitely, it flows. This is why fluids can be poured, pumped, and shaped by their containers.

A.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of pressure?
A.explain: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), which equals one newton per square metre (N/m²) One pascal is a very small pressure, about the pressure of a single sheet of paper resting on a table. Atmospheric pressure is about 101,300 Pa, and blood pressure is typically expressed in mmHg, where 1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa. The pascal is defined directly from force and area.

A.q: How much mass of fluid does a box of volume 0.25 m³ displace when fully submerged in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³)?
A.explain: m_f = ρV = 1000 × 0.25 = 250 kg of fluid displaced. The displaced mass generates the buoyant force: F_B = m_f g = 250 × 9.8 = 2450 N. That force does not depend on the object's own mass. A heavier object that is still fully submerged displaces the same 250 kg of water.

A.q: What is the buoyant force on a sphere of volume 0.40 m³ fully submerged in a fluid of density 800 kg/m³? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A.explain: F_B = ρgV = 800 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 3136 N. A fluid less dense than water (800 kg/m³, similar to some oils) gives less buoyancy than fresh water would for the same volume. Buoyancy scales linearly with fluid density, which is why an object that sinks in water can float in mercury.

A.q: A hydraulic press has a small piston of area 0.02 m² and a large piston of area 1.0 m². What output force results from an input force of 250 N?
A.explain: F_out = F_in × (A_out / A_in) = 250 × (1.0 / 0.02) = 250 × 50 = 12,500 N. The area ratio is 50:1, so the force multiplication is 50×. The small piston must travel 50 times farther than the large piston moves.

A.q: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 12 m in a lake (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)?
A.explain: P_G = ρgh = 1000 × 9.8 × 12 = 1.176 × 10⁵ Pa, about 1.2 atm of gauge pressure. The absolute pressure at that depth is P_atm + P_G = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 1.176 × 10⁵ = 2.189 × 10⁵ Pa. Gauge pressure is what most diving and plumbing gauges measure.

A.q: Convert a systolic pressure of 120 mmHg to pascals. (1 mmHg ≈ 133.3 Pa)
A.explain: 120 × 133.3 = 15,996 Pa ≈ 1.60 × 10⁴ Pa. A systolic pressure of 120 mmHg is about 16 kPa, much smaller than atmospheric pressure (101 kPa), which is why blood pressure is quoted in mmHg. A systolic of 120 mmHg is a typical healthy reading.

A.q: A wooden block floats in water with 30% of its volume submerged. If its total volume is 0.05 m³ and water density is 1000 kg/m³, what is the buoyant force on the block? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A.explain: Volume submerged = 0.30 × 0.05 = 0.015 m³. F_B = ρgV_sub = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.015 = 147 N. For a floating object the buoyant force equals the weight, so the block's mass is 147/9.8 = 15 kg. The 30% submergence means the wood's density is 30% of water's, 300 kg/m³.

A.q: What is the net upward force on a submerged object if its weight is 180 N and the buoyant force is 260 N?
A.explain: Net force = F_B − weight = 260 − 180 = 80 N upward. The object rises toward the surface. The buoyant force and the weight act in opposite directions, so they subtract; adding them, or reporting either force alone, is not the net force.

A.q: In a manometer connected to a gas container, the liquid on the container side is 18 cm lower than the liquid on the atmosphere side. If the liquid is mercury (ρ = 13,600 kg/m³) and g = 9.8 m/s², what is the gauge pressure of the gas?
A.explain: P_gauge = ρgΔh = 13,600 × 9.8 × 0.18 = 23,990 Pa ≈ 2.40 × 10⁴ Pa. The height difference is 18 cm = 0.18 m. Because mercury is so dense, a modest height difference is a large pressure, about 0.24 atm above atmospheric pressure. The same gauge pressure with water would need a column about 13.6 times taller, roughly 2.4 m.

A.q: Which of the following is the most convenient reason mercury is used in barometers instead of water?
options: Mercury has essentially no vapour pressure
Mercury costs less than water to obtain
Mercury's density keeps the column short
Mercury is safer to handle than water
A.explain: Mercury is about 13.6 times as dense as water, so a 1 atm column is about 0.76 m instead of 10.3 m. Cost and safety do not favour mercury, and a low vapour pressure is useful but not the reason the column is manageable.

A.q: How much does the gauge pressure increase for every 15 m of depth in fresh water? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²)
A.explain: Gauge pressure rises by ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 15 = 1.47×10⁵ Pa, about 147 kPa, close to 1.5 atm.

A.q: In Pascal's principle, if the area of the small piston is halved while the applied force stays the same, what happens to the pressure in the hydraulic fluid?
A.explain: P = F / A. Halving the area A with constant force F doubles the pressure The pressure is transmitted unchanged throughout the confined fluid, so doubling the input pressure doubles the output pressure. On the output side, this doubled pressure acts on the large piston and produces twice the output force. This is how reducing the input area amplifies the force multiplication of a hydraulic system.

A.q: Which of the following best explains why our cells are not crushed by atmospheric pressure?
options: Outside pressure is too small to crush cells
A vacuum shield keeps outside pressure off
Body tissues carry no pressure of their own
A.explain: Cells are not crushed because internal pressure matches the surrounding atmospheric pressure. Atmospheric pressure is large, the body is not in a vacuum, and tissues are not pressure-free.

A.q: A 0.50 m³ block floats in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m³) with 80% of its volume submerged. What is the buoyant force on the block? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A.explain: Volume submerged = 0.80 × 0.50 = 0.40 m³. F_B = ρgV_sub = 1025 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 4018 N. That equals the weight of the displaced seawater, not the weight of a fully submerged block. The 80% figure means the block's density is 0.80 × 1025 = 820 kg/m³.

A.q: The water barometer column is 10.40 m tall at 1 atm. If the local atmospheric pressure drops to 0.95 atm, what is the new column height?
A.explain: h ∝ P. New h = 10.40 × (0.95 / 1.00) = 9.88 m ≈ 9.9 m. A 5% drop in atmospheric pressure shortens the column by 5%. A falling barometer column marks a falling pressure, often ahead of storms.

A.q: A swimmer at 4 m depth in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) feels a certain absolute pressure. At what depth would the swimmer feel twice that absolute pressure? (Take P_atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s²)
A.explain: P_abs at 4 m = P_atm + ρgh = 1.013 × 10⁵ + (1000 × 9.8 × 4) = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 3.92 × 10⁴ = 1.405 × 10⁵ Pa. Twice that is 2.810 × 10⁵ Pa. Then 2.810 × 10⁵ = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 9800h, so 9800h = 1.797 × 10⁵ and h ≈ 18.3 m. Gauge pressure doubles when depth doubles, but absolute pressure does not: the surface already contributes 1 atm, so doubling the absolute pressure at 4 m needs about 18.3 m, not 8 m.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What are the two types of fluid flow?
A.explain: The two types of fluid flow taught here are streamline (also called laminar) and turbulent. Laminar flow is smooth and orderly in parallel layers; turbulent flow is disordered and swirling. Rotational/irrotational, steady/unsteady, and compressible/incompressible are other fluid classifications, not the pair asked for.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which statement best describes laminar blood flow?
options: Flow that always produces an audible murmur
Irregular swirling, with layers mixing freely
Smooth, orderly flow in parallel layers
Flow that occurs in veins and nowhere else
A.explain: Laminar flow is smooth and orderly, with blood moving in parallel layers. Swirls and murmurs belong to turbulence, and laminar flow is not limited to veins.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which statement best describes turbulent blood flow?
options: Smooth, orderly flow in parallel layers
Irregular swirling once speed is very high
Flow that is confined to the aorta
Flow with no energy loss or added resistance
A.explain: Turbulent flow is irregular swirling, and it appears when speed becomes very high. Parallel layers are laminar, the aorta is not the only site, and turbulence dissipates energy and raises resistance.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Normal blood flow in a healthy artery is:
options: A mix of laminar and turbulent
A.explain: Normal blood flow in a healthy artery is laminar: smooth and orderly. Turbulence appears when the vessel is narrowed or when velocity becomes very high. A healthy artery with normal flow maintains laminar conditions.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flow through a narrowed artery is expected to be:
A.explain: Blood flow through a narrowed artery becomes turbulent. Heart valve disease may also produce turbulence and heart murmurs The narrowing forces blood to speed up (continuity), and the high-speed jet passing through the narrow region disrupts the smooth parallel layers, producing turbulence. This is also why murmurs are heard with a stethoscope, the turbulent flow creates audible vibrations.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Mass flow rate is defined as: (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
options: The pressure divided by the area
The amount of volume passing a point per unit time
The amount of mass passing a given point per unit time
The force exerted by a fluid on the tube wall
A.explain: Mass flow rate is the amount of mass that passes a given point per unit time It is written as mass divided by time. The SI unit is kg/s. This is different from volume flow rate, which measures how much volume passes per unit time (m³/s). Both describe 'how much' passes, but one tracks mass and the other tracks volume.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is the correct final formula for mass flow rate? (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Mass flow rate = ρ A v, where ρ is density, A is cross-sectional area, and v is the velocity of the fluid Derivation: mass flow rate = mass / time = ρV / t = ρ(A × l) / t = ρA(l / t) = ρAv. The term l / t is the velocity v. Units check: kg/m³ × m² × m/s = kg/s.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Volume flow rate is calculated as:
A.explain: Volume flow rate Q = A v, where A is cross-sectional area and v is velocity Volume flow rate measures how much volume passes a point per unit time, with units m³/s. Mass flow rate is simply density × volume flow rate: mass flow rate = ρ × (A v) = ρ A v.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: The equation of continuity in its general form is:
options: ρ₁ A₁ v₁ = ρ₂ A₂ v₂
A.explain: As long as no fluid is added or removed, mass flow is conserved: ρ₁ A₁ v₁ = ρ₂ A₂ v₂. For an incompressible fluid the densities cancel to give A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂. ρ₁ / A₁ = ρ₂ / A₂ drops the velocity term, and Q = A / v inverts the volume-flow relation.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: For an incompressible fluid, the equation of continuity simplifies to:
A.explain: When density is constant (typical for liquids), the ρ terms cancel: A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂ Blood is essentially incompressible, so this simplified form applies directly to blood flow. It means that where the vessel is narrower, velocity must be higher, and where the vessel is wider, velocity must be lower, the product of area and velocity is preserved.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: A blood vessel narrows from A₁ = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m² (V₁ = 0.40 m/s) to A₂ = 5.0×10⁻⁵ m². What is V₂?
A.explain: Using A₁V₁ = A₂V₂: V₂ = (A₁V₁) / A₂ = (2.0×10⁻⁴ × 0.40) / 5.0×10⁻⁵ = 1.6 m/s. The area fell by a factor of 4, so the speed rose by the same factor, from 0.40 m/s to 1.6 m/s. That is why blood speeds up through a stenosis. The product A × v stays the same, not v alone.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In laminar flow, where is the velocity of the blood highest?
options: In the centre of the vessel
It is uniform across the vessel
A.explain: Velocity is highest in the centre of the vessel and lowest near the vessel wall. The profile is parabolic The layer right at the wall is essentially stationary (no-slip condition), while the fluid in the centre moves fastest. This is why the velocity profile in laminar flow looks like a parabola, a smooth curve from zero at the wall to maximum at the centre.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What is the velocity profile of laminar blood flow described as?
A.explain: Laminar blood flow has a parabolic velocity profile: highest in the centre, lowest near the wall. Layers slide past one another smoothly, peaking at the centre and tapering toward the wall. Flat, random, and rectangular profiles do not describe that laminar pattern.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In turbulent blood flow, how do the layers move?
options: Both radially and axially, so the layers mix
Neither radially nor axially, so layers stay put
Axially along the vessel, with no radial mixing
Radially across the vessel, with no axial motion
A.explain: In turbulent flow the layers mix and run both radially and axially. A stop, axial motion alone, or radial motion alone is not that mixed path.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is not a cause of turbulent blood flow?
options: A change in the speed of the blood
A stenosis narrowing the vessel lumen
A.explain: Turbulence is favoured by wall irregularity, a change in flow speed, or stenosis (narrowing) that speeds flow. A rise in blood temperature is not taught as a cause of turbulent blood flow in this unit.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is a consequence of turbulent blood flow?
options: Reduced energy loss in the vessel
A.explain: Turbulence wastes energy, raises resistance, can reduce tissue perfusion, and can produce a murmur. It does not cut energy loss, lower resistance, or speed nutrient delivery.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What is the difference between mass flow rate and volume flow rate? (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
options: Mass flow tracks volume per time; volume flow tracks mass per time
Mass flow and volume flow track one and the same quantity
Mass flow is reserved for gases; volume flow is reserved for liquids
Mass flow tracks mass per time; volume flow tracks volume per time
A.explain: Mass flow rate is mass per time, ρ A v. Volume flow rate is volume per time, A v. They are not the same quantity, not swapped, and not split by gas and liquid.

A.q: Three cubes have the same dimensions. Which has the highest density?
A.explain: Density is mass divided by volume. Equal dimensions mean equal volume, so the cube with the greatest mass has the greatest density. Gold is far denser than wood or paper, so the gold cube has the highest density. Equal size does not force equal density, and paper is the least dense of the three.

A.q: A wooden block measuring 5 cm × 4 cm × 8 cm has a mass of 80 g. What is its density?
A.explain: Volume is 5 × 4 × 8 = 160 cm³. Density is mass divided by volume, 80 / 160 = 0.50 g/cm³. The larger values divide volume by mass, or treat an edge as the density.

A.q: A wooden block has a mass of 30.0 g and dimensions 2.00 cm × 5.00 cm × 6.00 cm. What is its density?
A.explain: Volume is 2.00 × 5.00 × 6.00 = 60.0 cm³. Density is 30.0 / 60.0 = 0.500 g/cm³. 5.00 g/cm³ inverts the division, 60.0 g/cm³ is the volume written as a density, and 0.050 g/cm³ drops a factor of ten.

A.q: A plastic block measures 4 cm × 5 cm × 8 cm and has a density of 0.40 g/cm³. What is its mass?
A.explain: Volume is 4 × 5 × 8 = 160 cm³. Mass is density times volume, 0.40 × 160 = 64 g. 128 g uses twice the density, 17 g adds the edges, and 0.0025 g divides density by volume.

A.q: The pressure in a room is 1.215 × 10⁵ Pa. What force acts on a floor measuring 4 m × 5 m?
A.explain: Force is pressure times area. Area is 20 m², so F = 1.215 × 10⁵ × 20 = 2.43 × 10⁶ N.

A.q: A patient has a diastolic arterial pressure of 90 mmHg. What is this pressure in pascals? Take 760 mmHg = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
A.explain: 90 / 760 × 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 1.200 × 10⁴ Pa = 12.00 kPa. 16.00 kPa and 18.00 kPa scale 90 mmHg as if it were about 120 mmHg or 135 mmHg, and 3.00 kPa drops a factor of about four.

A.q: A patient has a systolic arterial pressure of 160 mmHg. What is this pressure in pascals? Take 760 mmHg = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
A.explain: 160 / 760 × 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 2.133 × 10⁴ Pa = 21.33 kPa. 10.66 kPa is half, 16.00 kPa treats 160 as 120 mmHg, and 28.40 kPa overscales the conversion.

A.q: A patient's systolic arterial pressure is 110 mmHg. What is this pressure in pascals? Take 760 mmHg = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
A.explain: 110 / 760 × 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 1.47 × 10⁴ Pa. 1.10 × 10⁵ Pa copies the millimetres of mercury into pascals with a wrong power, 7.60 × 10⁵ Pa inflates one atmosphere, and 1.013 × 10³ Pa is a truncated atmosphere.

A.q: What is the buoyant force on a box of volume 0.30 m³ fully submerged in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, ρ g V = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.30 = 2940 N, upward. 1000 N is the density written as a force, 2450 N uses a volume of 0.25 m³, and 5880 N doubles the volume.

A.q: A metal ball has a mass of 24 g and a density of 6.0 g/cm³. What is its volume?
A.explain: Volume is mass divided by density, 24 / 6.0 = 4.00 cm³. 2.40 cm³ uses a density of 10 g/cm³, 6.50 cm³ uses a density of about 3.7 g/cm³, and 10.2 cm³ subtracts density from mass.

A.q: How massive is a wooden block measuring 5 cm × 6 cm × 10 cm with a density of 0.40 g/cm³?
A.explain: Volume is 5 × 6 × 10 = 300 cm³. Mass is 0.40 × 300 = 120 g. 75 g uses a density of 0.25 g/cm³, 21 g adds the edges, and 48 g uses a volume of 120 cm³.

A.q: Air pressure in a room is 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa and the air exerts a force of 3.60 × 10⁵ N on a table. What is the area of the table?
A.explain: Area is force divided by pressure, 3.60 × 10⁵ / 1.20 × 10⁵ = 3.0 m². 6.0 m² and 12 m² drop a factor of two or four, and 1.8 m² divides the leading digits the wrong way.

A.q: A pressure gauge on a diver reads 1.96 × 10⁵ Pa in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³. How deep is the diver? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Depth is gauge pressure divided by ρ g, 1.96 × 10⁵ / (1000 × 9.8) = 20.0 m. The smaller depths divide by 2 g, by about 1.3 g, or use g = 12.

A.q: A buoyant force of 1960 N acts on a box fully submerged in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³. What is the volume of the box? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Volume is buoyant force divided by ρ g, 1960 / (1000 × 9.8) = 0.20 m³. 2.00 m³ divides by 100 g, 20.0 m³ divides by 10 g, and 39.2 m³ divides by 50.

A.q: What absolute pressure acts on a swimmer 25 m below the surface of fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³? Take atmospheric pressure as 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Absolute pressure is atmospheric pressure plus ρ g h. ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 25 = 2.45 × 10⁵ Pa, so P = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 2.45 × 10⁵ = 3.463 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.46 × 10⁵ Pa. 1.46 × 10⁵ Pa understates the water column, and the 10⁶ Pa values multiply depth by an extra factor of ten.

A.q: A hydraulic press has a large piston of area 0.25 m² and a small piston of area 0.05 m². What force on the small piston lifts a 2000 N object?
A.explain: Pascal's principle keeps F/A the same, so F_small = 2000 × (0.05 / 0.25) = 400 N. 80 N and 200 N use area ratios of 1/25 and 1/10, and 500 N uses a ratio of 0.25.

A.q: What gauge pressure does fresh water produce at a depth of 6.0 m? Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Gauge pressure is ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 6.0 = 58800 Pa. 9800 Pa drops the depth, 60 Pa drops both density factors, and 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa is standard atmospheric pressure rather than the water column.

A.q: A room is at 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa. What force does this pressure exert on a table measuring 2 m × 4 m?
A.explain: Area is 8 m², so force is 1.25 × 10⁵ × 8 = 1.00 × 10⁶ N. 1.25 × 10⁵ N ignores the area, 6.25 × 10⁴ N divides by one side, and 2.50 × 10⁴ N divides by a side of 5 m.

A.q: A diver's gauge pressure is 1.96 × 10⁵ Pa in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³. How deep is the diver? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Depth is 1.96 × 10⁵ / (1000 × 9.8) = 20.0 m. 0.0200 m and 2.00 m drop powers of ten, and 200 m multiplies by ten.

A.q: At a depth of 500 m in water of density 1000 kg/m³, with atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s², which pair of pressures is correct?
options: Gauge pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and absolute pressure 4.90 × 10⁶ Pa
Gauge pressure 4.90 × 10⁶ Pa and absolute pressure 5.00 × 10⁶ Pa
Gauge pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and absolute pressure 4.90 × 10⁵ Pa
Gauge pressure 4.90 × 10⁶ Pa and absolute pressure 4.90 × 10⁵ Pa
A.explain: Gauge pressure is ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 500 = 4.90 × 10⁶ Pa. Absolute pressure adds the atmosphere, 4.90 × 10⁶ + 1.01 × 10⁵ = 5.001 × 10⁶ Pa ≈ 5.00 × 10⁶ Pa. A gauge value of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa is the atmosphere alone, and an absolute value of 4.90 × 10⁵ Pa drops a factor of ten.

A.q: A hydraulic lift has a large piston of area 0.20 m² and a small piston of area 0.020 m². What force on the small piston lifts a 2400 N object?
A.explain: F_small = 2400 × (0.020 / 0.20) = 240 N. 24 N drops a factor of ten, 24000 N inverts the area ratio, and 2400 N assumes the areas are equal.

A.q: What is the buoyant force on a fully submerged box of volume 0.40 m³ in fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³? Take g = 9.8 m/s².
A.explain: Buoyant force is ρ g V = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 3920 N, directed upward. 7840 N uses a volume of 0.80 m³, 392 N drops a factor of ten, and 400 N downward has both the wrong magnitude and the wrong direction.

A.q: Which of the following is an SI base quantity with its correct SI unit?
A.explain: Mass is one of the seven SI base quantities, and its unit is the kilogram. Energy, pressure, and force are derived quantities: the joule, the pascal, and the newton are built from base units, so a correct unit name does not make them base quantities.

A.q: Which medical set is matched to the correct state of matter?
options: Bone as solid, blood as gas, air in the lungs as liquid
Bone as gas, blood as liquid, air in the lungs as solid
Bone as solid, blood as liquid, air in the lungs as gas
Bone as liquid, blood as solid, air in the lungs as gas
A.explain: Bone keeps a definite shape and volume, so it is solid. Blood flows and takes the shape of its vessel while keeping a nearly fixed volume, so it is liquid. Air in the lungs expands to fill the available space, so it is gas.

A.q: When does shear stress occur in a material?
options: When force acts perpendicular to the surface
When force acts parallel to the surface
When pressure acts equally in all directions
When force acts vertically downward only
A.explain: Shear stress is a tangential force per unit area, so the force is parallel to the surface and tends to slide layers past each other. A perpendicular force is longitudinal stress, equal pressure from all sides is hydraulic stress, and a downward force is not shear unless it is parallel to the face being considered.

A.q: A force of 180 N acts over an area of 0.020 m². What stress is produced?
A.explain: Stress is force divided by area, 180 / 0.020 = 9000 Pa. 9 Pa inverts the division, 180 Pa ignores the area, and 1800 Pa uses an area of 0.10 m².

A.q: A cortical bone has Young's modulus 20 × 10⁹ Pa and is subjected to a stress of 50 × 10⁶ Pa. What strain is produced?
A.explain: Within the elastic limit, strain is stress divided by Young's modulus, 50 × 10⁶ / 20 × 10⁹ = 0.0025. 0.00025 drops a factor of ten, 0.0050 uses a modulus of 10 × 10⁹ Pa, and 0.025 inverts a power of ten.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flows through a vessel of cross-sectional area 3.0×10⁻⁴ m² at 0.30 m/s. The vessel narrows to 1.0×10⁻⁴ m². What is the new speed, if the fluid is incompressible?
A.explain: Continuity for an incompressible fluid gives A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = 3.0×10⁻⁴ × 0.30 / 1.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.90 m/s. 0.10 m/s inverts the area ratio, 0.30 m/s assumes speed is unchanged, and 2.7 m/s uses a ratio of 9.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which pair of conditions can raise blood speed or otherwise favour turbulent flow?
options: A narrowed vessel, and a damaged or irregular valve
No blood movement, and a perfectly uniform vessel
A narrowed vessel, and a perfectly uniform vessel of unchanged area
A damaged valve, and a complete absence of blood movement
A.explain: A narrowed vessel raises speed by continuity, and a damaged or irregular valve disturbs the layers. Both favour turbulence. Absence of movement cannot raise speed, and a uniform vessel of unchanged area does not add the geometric trigger.

A.q: Which statement correctly separates matter from light?
options: Matter has no mass, but it still occupies space
Solids alone are matter, and light is matter too
Light is matter, because it occupies space
Matter has mass and occupies space, unlike light
A.explain: Matter has mass and occupies space. Light carries energy and can fill a region, but it has no rest mass and is not matter. A massless object, a solids-only rule, and treating light as matter each fail that split.

A.q: Which state of matter has both a definite shape and a definite volume?
options: Plasma, with no fixed shape or volume
A liquid, with fixed volume and no fixed shape
A solid, with fixed shape and fixed volume
A gas, with neither fixed shape nor volume
A.explain: A solid keeps both its shape and its volume. A liquid keeps volume but takes the container's shape, a gas keeps neither, and plasma likewise has no fixed shape or volume.

A.q: Which pairing of intermolecular force and diffusion rate is correct?
options: Force strongest in solids, and diffusion fastest in solids
Force strongest in gases, and diffusion fastest in solids
Force strongest in solids, and diffusion fastest in gases
Force strongest in gases, and diffusion fastest in gases
A.explain: Intermolecular force runs solid, then liquid, then gas. Diffusion runs the other way: gas, then liquid, then solid.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which feature most clearly marks turbulent flow rather than laminar flow?
options: It appears when the speed is very low
It contains irregular swirls and eddies
It dissipates no energy as the fluid moves
It keeps every layer moving in a straight path
A.explain: Turbulent flow is irregular, with swirls and eddies and mixing between layers. Low speed, no energy loss, and straight layers belong to laminar flow, not turbulence.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Under ordinary resting conditions in a healthy person, blood flow is usually:
options: Vapor flow, with no liquid motion
No flow at all in the arteries
A.explain: At rest in a healthy artery, blood moves in smooth parallel layers, which is laminar flow. It is not vapor, not stationary, and not turbulent in every vessel.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In steady flow, with no fluid added or removed, what stays the same between two points?
options: The fluid temperature at both points
The vessel diameter at both points
The fluid speed at both points
The flow rate at both points
A.explain: If nothing is added or removed, the flow rate into one section equals the flow rate out of the next. Temperature, diameter, and speed can all change along the path.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: The cross-section of an incompressible vessel falls by a factor of 5. By what factor does the speed rise, in steady flow?
A.explain: For an incompressible fluid, area times speed is constant, so speed rises by the same factor that area falls. A drop by 5 raises speed by 5, not by 2, 10, or 25.

A.q: Loss of elasticity in blood-vessel walls is linked with which outcome?
options: A rise in bone stiffness and fracture resistance
A fall in blood density with no vessel change
Cardiovascular disease from stiffer vessel walls
A change of blood from liquid into a gas
A.explain: When vessel walls lose elasticity they stiffen, and that loss is linked with cardiovascular disease. Bone stiffness, blood density, and a change of state are not that vessel effect.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which body fluids are liquids, and which are gases, in the circulation and the airway?
options: Blood, lymph, and plasma as liquids; oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air as gases
Blood, lymph, and plasma as gases; oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air as liquids
Blood and airway air as liquids; lymph, plasma, and oxygen as gases
Plasma and carbon dioxide as liquids; blood, lymph, and oxygen as gases
A.explain: Blood, lymph, and plasma are liquids. Oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air in the airway are gases. Swapping the two groups, or splitting one group across both states, breaks that pairing.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood is treated as which kind of fluid in the continuity relation used for vessels?
options: A gas whose density falls as it speeds up
A solid that keeps a fixed vessel shape
An incompressible liquid of steady density
A fluid whose density doubles in a narrow segment
A.explain: Blood is treated as incompressible, so density stays the same and continuity reduces to area times speed. A gas that thins, a solid, or a density that doubles would not give that reduction.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In carotid stenosis, why does blood speed rise in the narrowed segment?
options: Hooke's relation stretches the wall, and speed follows the stretch
The continuity relation keeps area times speed constant
Pascal's relation sends the same pressure to every point
Archimedes' relation equals the upward force to displaced weight
A.explain: Speed rises because the narrower area must carry the same flow, so area times speed stays constant. Hooke, Pascal and Archimedes do not set that speed.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flows at 0.20 m/s through a vessel of area 0.030 m². The vessel narrows to 0.010 m². What is the new speed, if the blood is incompressible?
A.explain: Area times speed is constant, so 0.030 × 0.20 = 0.010 × v₂. That gives v₂ = 0.60 m/s.

A.q: Match each modulus to the strain in its formula.

rightItems.text: Change in length over original length
Change in volume over original volume

A.explain: Young's modulus uses longitudinal strain, ΔL/L. Shear modulus uses shear strain, Δx/L. Bulk modulus uses volume strain, ΔV/V. Force times length is not a strain.

A.q: Match each stress to the way the force is applied.

rightItems.text: Along the long axis of the object
Inward from all sides at once
At a single point on the face

A.explain: Longitudinal stress pulls or pushes along the axis. Shear stress acts parallel to the face. Hydraulic stress is a uniform pressure from all sides. A single point force is none of the three.

A.q: Match each mechanical property to the change it names.
A.explain: Elasticity recovers shape. Plasticity leaves a permanent set. Ductility is drawing into wire. Malleability is hammering into sheet. A volume that does not change is compressibility's opposite, not one of these four.

A.q: Match each state to its shape and volume.

rightItems.text: No fixed shape and no fixed volume

A.explain: A solid keeps shape and volume. A liquid keeps volume and takes the container's shape. A gas keeps neither. A fixed shape with no fixed volume is not one of the three.

A.q: Match each base quantity, named by its unit system, to the unit that system uses.
A.explain: SI and MKS share the metre and the kilogram. CGS uses the centimetre and the gram. FPS uses the foot and the pound. Time is the second in all four systems.

A.q: Match each pressure term to the relation that defines it.

rightItems.text: The pressure of the air at the surface

A.explain: Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. Gauge pressure is absolute minus atmospheric. Atmospheric pressure is the surface air pressure. Pressure at a depth is density times g times depth. Force times area is not a pressure.

A.q: Match each measured quantity to the unit used for it.
A.explain: Stress is force per area, so its unit is the pascal. A mercury column is read in millimetres of mercury. Force is the newton. Density is the kilogram per cubic metre. Strain is a ratio, so it has no unit. The joule is energy.

A.q: Match each symbol to the quantity it stands for. (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Capital V is volume and small v is velocity. ρ is density. σ is stress and ε is strain. The dotted m, ṁ, is mass flow rate. Q is volume flow rate.

A.q: Match each solid-mechanics formula to the quantity it defines.
A.explain: Stress is force over area. Longitudinal strain is the change in length over the original length. Dividing that stress by that strain gives Young's modulus. Shear and bulk modulus use sideways shift and volume change in the same place. Density is mass over volume. Force times area is not one of these.

A.q: Match each fluid formula to the quantity it defines. (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Pressure is force over area. Gauge pressure at a depth is density times g times depth. Absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure to the gauge reading. Buoyant force is the weight of the displaced fluid, ρgV. The small-piston force is the large force times the small area over the large area. Mass flow rate is ρAv and volume flow rate is Av.

A.q: Match each required quantity to the rearrangement that gives it.
A.explain: Force is pressure times area, not pressure divided by area. The small-piston force is the large force times the small area over the large area. Dividing by the large area twice, or swapping the areas, does not give it. Narrow-segment speed is the incoming area-speed product divided by the narrow area. Compression is stress times length divided by Young's modulus. Density is mass divided by volume.

A.q: Match each point on a tensile test to what the specimen is doing there.

rightItems.text: Last point of full shape recovery

A.explain: Up to the proportional limit, stress stays proportional to strain. The elastic limit is the last point at which the shape fully returns. Past that, the plastic region leaves a permanent set. The breaking point is fracture. Melting is a thermal change, not a point on this curve.

A.q: Match each unit to the class of quantity it belongs to.
A.explain: The metre, the kilogram, and the second are base units, for length, mass, and time. The newton, the pascal, and the metre per second are derived units, for force, pressure, and velocity.

A.q: Compared with an amorphous solid, a crystalline solid has particles in a repeating long-range ordered lattice. Which mechanical / thermal contrast best matches that structural difference?
options: Crystalline solids melt sharply; amorphous solids soften over a range
Crystalline solids have no fixed positions; amorphous solids form a lattice
Amorphous solids are always more ductile than crystalline metals lacking order
Both solid types flow like a liquid while keeping a sharp melting point
A.explain: Crystalline solids have a repeating pattern through the whole material, so they usually melt at a clear temperature. Amorphous solids (like glass) are more jumbled, so they soften gradually as they warm up. Being crystalline does not make something brittle — many metals are crystalline and still bend — and neither type of solid flows like a liquid.

A.q: Which description fits particle motion in a flowing liquid?
options: Particles slide past one another and have no rigid lattice
Particles stay locked in a repeating lattice
Particles have no fixed position and fill the whole container
Particles are randomly distributed with no contact at all
A.explain: In a liquid the particles slide past one another, which is what lets the liquid flow, and they are not locked in a lattice. Filling the container with no fixed position is the gas. A total absence of contact is not the liquid.

A.q: Which description fits the particles of a gas?
options: Locked in a lattice, with fixed positions
Sliding in contact, taking the container's shape only
Rapid and random, with no fixed position, filling the container
Ordered in a crystal, filling only the bottom of the container
A.explain: Gas particles move rapidly and at random, have no fixed position, and fill the container. A lattice is a solid. Sliding in contact and taking the container's shape, without filling it, is a liquid.

A.q: Which state takes the shape of the container, and which state fills the container?
options: Liquid takes the shape; gas fills the container
Gas takes the shape only; liquid fills the container
Solid takes the shape; liquid fills the container
Solid fills the container; gas keeps its own shape
A.explain: A liquid takes the container's shape and keeps its own volume. A gas fills the container. A solid keeps both shape and volume.

A.q: A rubber band or a spring returns to its old shape after the load is removed. Which property is that?
A.explain: Return to the original shape is elasticity. Plasticity is the permanent set left by repeated loading. Ductility is drawing into wire, and malleability is hammering into sheet.

A.q: A rubber band or a spring is loaded repeatedly until it no longer returns to its old shape. Which property is that?
A.explain: A permanent change of shape after repeated loading is plasticity. Elasticity would have returned the shape. Ductility and malleability name drawing into wire and hammering into sheet.

A.q: Silver, gold, lead, and tin can be drawn into wire. Which property is that?
A.explain: Drawing into wire is ductility, and silver, gold, lead, and tin show it. Elasticity recovers shape, plasticity is a permanent set, and malleability is hammering into sheet.

A.q: A force along the length of a rod, and a force parallel to a face, are which pair of stresses?
A.explain: A force along the length is longitudinal stress. A force parallel to a face is shear stress, the horizontal slide. Hydraulic stress comes from all sides, and the swapped pair reverses the two loadings.

A.q: A density of 1 g/cm³ is equal to which value in kg/m³?
A.explain: One gram is 10⁻³ kg and one cubic centimetre is 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g/cm³ = 10⁻³ / 10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg/m³. Multiply the number in g/cm³ by 1000.

A.q: Standard atmospheric pressure is 101325 Pa. Which reading is the same pressure?
A.explain: 101325 Pa is 1.01325 × 10⁵ Pa, which is 1 atm, and 1 atm supports 760 mm of mercury. A 76 mm column, a 1013 mm column, and a 10.3 mm column are not that reading. A water column for the same pressure is about 10.3 m, not 10.3 mm.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Mass flow rate is written Q = m/Δt, with m the mass. Which unit does that expression give? (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Mass divided by time is the kilogram per second. Cubic metre per second is volume flow rate. Kilogram metre per second is momentum, and the newton-second is impulse (not mass flow rate).

A.q: Match each derived quantity, named by its unit system, to the unit that system uses.
A.explain: SI and MKS share the newton for force and the pascal for pressure. CGS uses the dyne, and the dyne per square centimetre. FPS uses the pound-force, and the pound per square inch. The joule is energy, not force or pressure.

A.q: Match each phase change to the correct state transition.
A.explain: Melting is solid→liquid; freezing is liquid→solid; vaporization is liquid→gas; condensation is gas→liquid; sublimation is solid→gas directly; deposition is gas→solid directly (e.g. CO₂ forming dry ice). These six names are the standard phase-change set.

A.q: Which phase change is solid to gas directly, without becoming a liquid first?
A.explain: Sublimation is solid→gas directly. Melting is solid→liquid; condensation is gas→liquid; deposition is gas→solid directly.

A.q: A metal block measures 3.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm and has a mass of 360 g. Taking the density of water as 1.0 g/cm³, what is the specific gravity of the metal?
A.explain: Volume = 3.0 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 60 cm³. Density = 360 / 60 = 6.0 g/cm³. Specific gravity = ρ_substance / ρ_water = 6.0 / 1.0 = 6.0 (dimensionless). 0.167 inverts mass/volume; 3.0 undercounts the volume product; 12 doubles the density.

A.q: An open-tube water manometer connected to a gas container shows a height difference Δh = 40 cm, with the container-side level lower. If ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², and P_atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, what is the absolute pressure of the gas?
A.explain: Gauge pressure = ρgΔh = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 3920 Pa. Absolute pressure = P_atm + P_gauge = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 3920 = 1.0522 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 1.052 × 10⁵ Pa. 3.92 × 10³ Pa is the gauge pressure alone; 9.74 × 10⁴ Pa subtracts gauge from atm; 1.405 × 10⁵ Pa treats the column as 4 m rather than 0.40 m.
